key_question: How do the geographies of England and Brazil compare?
challenge: Can you explain what makes these two countries so different?

lessons.what: to locate England and Brazil on a world map and describe their positions
lessons.why: geographers always begin by asking where a place is and what they expect to find there
lessons.success: locating both countries on a blank world map and writing two predictions about how they might differ

vocabulary.definition: one half of the Earth, divided either at the Equator (north/south) or the Prime Meridian (east/west)
imaginary lines running from the North Pole to the South Pole, measuring distance east or west of the Prime Meridian
imaginary lines running east to west around the Earth, measuring distance north or south of the Equator
one of the seven large land masses on Earth (e.g. South America, Europe)
the imaginary line at 0° latitude that divides the Earth into the northern and southern hemispheres

slides.title: Where on Earth are England and Brazil?
slides.content: England sits in north-west Europe at around 52°N, 1°W. Brazil dominates the eastern side of South America, straddling the Equator between 5°N and 33°S. Because Brazil is so large, parts of it are in both the northern and southern hemispheres.

slides.title: Locating both countries together
slides.content: Using an atlas, find and label England and Brazil on a blank world map. Mark the Equator, the Tropic of Capricorn, and the Prime Meridian. Write the approximate latitude and longitude of London and Brasília.

slides.title: Where in the world?
slides.content: Complete the world map independently, adding compass directions and a key. Write three geographical facts about the position of each country.

lessons.what: to identify and describe the main physical features of Brazil
lessons.why: understanding the physical landscape helps us explain the climate, wildlife and how people live
lessons.success: labelling the Amazon River, Amazon Rainforest, Cerrado savanna and Atlantic coast on a map of Brazil

vocabulary.definition: a dense forest found in tropical areas with very high rainfall throughout the year
a tropical grassland with scattered trees, found between the rainforest and drier regions
a smaller river or stream that flows into a larger river
a large area of land drained by a river and its tributaries
the height of land above sea level

quiz.question: On which continent is Brazil?
quiz.answer: South America

quiz.question: What is the name of the world's largest tropical rainforest, found mostly in Brazil?
quiz.answer: The Amazon Rainforest

quiz.question: What is the name of the world's largest river by volume, which flows through Brazil?
quiz.answer: The Amazon River

quiz.question: In which hemisphere is most of Brazil?
quiz.answer: The southern hemisphere

quiz.question: What is a savanna?
quiz.answer: A tropical grassland with scattered trees

slides.title: Brazil's major physical features
slides.content: Brazil has three main physical regions: the Amazon Basin in the north (home to the world's largest rainforest), the central Cerrado savanna plateau, and the Atlantic coast with its mountains. The Amazon River carries more water than any other river on Earth.

slides.title: Mapping Brazil's physical features
slides.content: Using your atlas, label the Amazon Basin, Amazon River, Cerrado, Serra do Mar mountains and the Atlantic Ocean on a map of Brazil. Add a colour-coded key showing land use and vegetation zones.

slides.title: Describing Brazil's landscape
slides.content: Write a paragraph describing Brazil's physical geography. Include: the Amazon Basin, at least two other physical features, and an explanation of how Brazil's position near the Equator affects its climate.

lessons.what: to identify and describe the main physical features of England
lessons.why: comparing England's landscape with Brazil's helps us understand how location and climate shape a country
lessons.success: labelling key rivers, upland regions and lowland areas on a map of England and writing a comparison sentence

vocabulary.definition: high, hilly or mountainous land, often found in the north and west of England
flat or gently rolling land, usually found in the south and east of England
the wide mouth of a river where it meets the sea and tidal water flows in and out
open, high land covered with heather, grasses and peat, common in northern England
flat land beside a river that floods when the river overflows its banks

quiz.question: What is the name of England's longest river?
quiz.answer: The River Severn

quiz.question: In which part of England do you find the highest land — north/west or south/east?
quiz.answer: North and west

quiz.question: What is an upland area?
quiz.answer: High, hilly or mountainous land

quiz.question: Name one upland region in England.
quiz.answer: The Pennines, Lake District, Dartmoor or Exmoor

quiz.question: What is a floodplain?
quiz.answer: Flat land beside a river that floods when the river overflows

slides.title: England's physical regions
slides.content: England's landscape divides into upland areas in the north and west — the Pennines, Lake District and Dartmoor — and flat lowlands in the south and east. Major rivers include the Severn, Thames and Trent. Unlike Brazil, England has a temperate maritime climate with mild, rainy winters and cool summers.

slides.title: Mapping England's physical features
slides.content: On a blank map of England, label the Pennines, Lake District, Thames, Severn, and the North Sea. Use an atlas to add spot heights for the highest points. Discuss with your partner: how does England's landscape differ from Brazil's?

slides.title: England's physical features
slides.content: Complete the annotated map of England. Then write a paragraph comparing England's physical geography with Brazil's. Use geographical vocabulary from this lesson and the last.

lessons.lesson_title: How do people live in England and Brazil?
lessons.what: to compare population, settlement patterns and land use in England and Brazil
lessons.why: physical geography shapes where and how people choose to live, work and travel
lessons.success: creating a comparison table showing at least four differences in how people live in England and Brazil

vocabulary.definition: the number of people living in a given area, usually measured per square kilometre
the process by which more people move from the countryside to live in cities
an informal settlement or shanty town found on the edges of Brazilian cities
a city with a population of more than ten million people
the way in which land in an area is used, for example for farming, housing or industry

quiz.question: What is population density?
quiz.answer: The number of people living per square kilometre

quiz.question: Name the largest city in Brazil.
quiz.answer: São Paulo

quiz.question: What is a favela?
quiz.answer: An informal settlement on the edges of Brazilian cities

quiz.question: What is urbanisation?
quiz.answer: The movement of people from the countryside to cities

quiz.question: Which city is the capital of Brazil?
quiz.answer: Brasília

slides.title: Comparing settlements and population
slides.content: Brazil has a population of about 215 million; England has about 57 million. However, Brazil is 35 times larger. Brazil's population is concentrated in coastal cities like São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Recife, while the interior Amazon region is very sparsely settled. England's population clusters in cities like London, Birmingham and Manchester.

slides.title: Fieldwork: reading settlement maps
slides.content: Compare population density maps of England and Brazil. Identify three areas of high density and three areas of low density in each country. Discuss why populations are concentrated where they are — think about physical features, rivers and trade routes.

slides.title: People and places comparison
slides.content: Create a comparison table with columns for England and Brazil. Include: population, capital city, largest city, main type of land use, and one example of a settlement challenge. Write a conclusion sentence explaining the most striking difference.

lessons.what: to draw conclusions about the similarities and differences between England and Brazil
lessons.why: communicating findings clearly is a key geographical skill and helps others understand the world better
lessons.success: writing a structured conclusion that answers the enquiry question using evidence from lessons 1 to 4

vocabulary.definition: a reasoned judgement you reach after looking at all the evidence
facts, data or examples that support an argument or claim
looking at two or more things to find similarities and differences
the effect one thing has on another, for example how climate influences vegetation
using resources in a way that meets our needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs

quiz.question: Name one physical similarity between England and Brazil.
quiz.answer: Both have major rivers (Thames/Severn and Amazon/São Francisco)

quiz.question: Name one physical difference between England and Brazil.
quiz.answer: Brazil has tropical rainforest; England has temperate moorland and farmland

quiz.question: Name one human geography difference.
quiz.answer: Brazil has megacities with favelas; England's cities are more evenly developed

quiz.question: How does Brazil's position near the Equator affect its climate?
quiz.answer: It makes the climate hot and wet, supporting tropical rainforest

quiz.question: What is our enquiry question?
quiz.answer: How do the geographies of England and Brazil compare?

slides.title: Answering our enquiry question
slides.content: England and Brazil are very different: Brazil is vast, tropical and dominated by the Amazon; England is small, temperate and heavily farmed. Yet both have major river systems, diverse landscapes and large urban populations. Geography — location, climate and landforms — shapes everything else about these countries.

slides.title: Building our conclusion together
slides.content: Using your notes from lessons 1 to 4, work with your partner to list three key similarities and three key differences between England and Brazil. Think about: physical features, climate, population and settlement. Rank them from most important to least important and be ready to explain your choices.

slides.title: Our enquiry conclusion
slides.content: Write a conclusion to our enquiry question: 'How do the geographies of England and Brazil compare?' Your answer should be at least three paragraphs: one on physical geography, one on human geography, and one overall judgement. Use geographical vocabulary and evidence from your work across the enquiry.
